source.version_note: Supplied arXiv:2603.11821v3 dated 28 September 2026 carries MELBA article layout, DOI and a journal publication date of 13 March 2026. This exact supplied revision was read; it extends previously reported 2025 experimental data, not a new independent sample for every publication.

citation.title: Stuck on Suggestions: Automation Bias, the Anchoring Effect, and the Factors That Shape Them in Computational Pathology
citation.venue: Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging, volume 2026, 126–147; supplied arXiv:2603.11821v3

reading.source_scope_note: Twenty-eight pathology professionals estimated tumor-cell percentages with and without image-model advice. This is human use of AI, not direct evidence of a model's own advice discounting or anchoring. Earlier 2025 reports share the experiment; cited original advice-taking studies were not independently read.
access_limits: All twenty-two pages read, including model architecture, sampling, thresholds, equations, study design, results, figures/captions, limitations, declarations, references and Appendix A. Page 13 Table 3 and page 22 Table 4 also rendered and visually inspected.

External supplemental datasets, participant records, analysis code and platform repository were not retrieved or rerun. Harmless pdftotext font warning did not prevent extraction; tables were visually checked.

study.design: Within participants: all unaided assessments first, then AI-assisted after two-week interval; ten images per round under ten-second countdown, randomized time-pressure starting set/order
study.model: FCOS detector with ResNet-18, trained on BreCaHad; tumor versus other cell counts form a percentage; tissue patches from three datasets
study.measures: Mean absolute percentage error, threshold-crossing negative consultations at 25%, normalized weight of advice, regression coefficients, experience and pre/post-advice confidence

summary: AI-assisted rounds had lower mean absolute estimation error overall, but 38/560 estimates crossed from correct to incorrect relative to the 25% threshold while AI was also wrong. Nineteen such events occurred in each time-pressure condition; larger mean errors under time pressure in that selected subset are descriptive. Advice influence is clear, but a positive AI regression weight does not alone establish disproportionate or harmful anchoring. Context and calibration remain essential.

findings.definition: Giving external advice less weight than one's own initial judgment when forming a revised judgment.
findings.novelty_rationale: Explicitly named in the paper's advice-taking discussion. Distinct from effort discounting, dismissing positive evidence, algorithm aversion (AI versus human source preference) and judging one's own outputs more favourably. It describes advice integration; whether the weighting is biased requires evidence about relative reliability.

evidence.quote: individuals still weigh their own assessments more heavily
people typically adjust only about 30% toward external

findings.evidence_scope: The general construct and 30% benchmark are reported from cited literature, not an independently read original study. The present experiment's aggregate final-estimate model gives own estimate coefficient .55 and AI coefficient .44; quality-stratified results give much greater AI weight for better advice than worse advice. No matched human-advisor condition establishes algorithm-specific discounting.
findings.boundary: Discounting is not inherently irrational. Own and external information may differ in precision, independence, relevance and access. A 50/50 or historical 30% weighting is not a universal optimal benchmark. Do not infer egocentric motive, subjective belief or poor calibration merely from a coefficient below one half.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Advice-taking construct discussed and illustrated in human AI-assisted judgments; model advice-integration analogue untested
findings.ai_proposal: Untested AI analogue: give an assistant an initial estimate and independent advice with explicitly known reliability. Measure how it updates as relative precision and evidence quality vary. Compare against a justified calibration target rather than require equal weights; distinguish source-identity preference from underweighting evidence.

findings.term: Some correct pathology estimates became wrong despite aggregate AI benefits
findings.definition: The AI-assisted round improved overall percentage-estimation error while including cases where an initially correct threshold classification became incorrect in the direction of faulty AI advice.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds expert task evidence and denominator/causal limits to an existing concept; a harmful consultation is not a separately named independent bias.

evidence.quote: reliance on automation is not inherently undesirable.

findings.evidence_scope: 38 negative and 29 positive threshold-crossing consultations among 560 AI-assisted assessments. The negative rate is about 6.8% of all assessments, not of all initially correct cases exposed to wrong advice. No inferential test of frequency/severity was performed after filtering.
findings.boundary: A before/after threshold reversal does not prove blind trust or uniquely isolate a causal automation mechanism. All AI rounds came second; practice, recollection and ordinary repeat variability remain possible. Aggregate error improvement and specific failures can coexist; no patient was treated or harmed in this study.

findings.term: Advice influence is not automatically disproportionate anchoring
findings.definition: Final estimates reflected both initial human and AI values, but nonzero AI weighting alone does not establish an irrational anchor or insufficient adjustment.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retains the paper's measured advice effects while qualifying its interpretation of any positive AI coefficient as anchoring bias.

evidence.quote: the judge and advisor are not independent,

findings.evidence_scope: Overall regression coefficients own estimate .55, AI .44. Appendix coefficients AI .74 when advice is closer to the reference and .30 when worse, showing some quality sensitivity. No optimal reliability-weighting benchmark or irrelevant randomized anchor is supplied.
findings.boundary: The human and AI inspect related image evidence; advice weights are not independent causal shares. The model does not constrain weights to sum to one, and normalized absolute-distance advice weighting loses direction and can hide overshooting. Beneficial use of more accurate advice must not be counted as a bias solely because a coefficient is positive.

findings.term: Time pressure changed advice reliance, while negative-consultation frequency stayed descriptive
findings.definition: A ten-second countdown increased the normalized advice-reliance measure, while observed negative-consultation counts were identical across time conditions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds task-specific time/accuracy evidence to the existing speed–accuracy trade-off rather than claim that time stress universally increases automation-bias occurrence.
findings.evidence_scope: Mean normalized reliance .48 without versus .54 with time pressure, paired two-sided p=.017. Both groups of assessments have 19/280 negative consultations; their mean absolute error 19.42 versus 27.79 is a selected-subset descriptive difference. Separate AI-slope estimates .41 versus .48 do not themselves test a slope interaction.
findings.boundary: A countdown is one temporal manipulation, not measured cognitive load or routine workload. The overall time main effect p=.19 and AI×time interaction p=.46 were not significant. Do not promote a one-tailed baseline-only comparison or a descriptive severity difference to a universal causal harm claim.

findings.term: Confidence with assistance is distinct from confidence before advice
findings.definition: Higher post-advice confidence correlated with greater advice reliance, whereas the baseline-confidence coefficient was negative and borderline.
findings.novelty_rationale: Distinguishes timing, observed confidence and calibration rather than infer overconfidence from increased confidence alone.
findings.evidence_scope: Table 3: baseline confidence β=−.03, p=.050, CI [−.07,.00]; assisted confidence β=.08, p<.001, CI [.04,.12]. Mean confidence rose 3.30 to 3.64 while overall error fell. Experience association β=−.06 is observational and coded on four ordered bins.
findings.boundary: A confidence increase alongside accuracy improvement is not by itself overconfidence. Post-choice confidence may follow agreement rather than cause it. Baseline confidence is a task-specific proxy, not a full self-efficacy trait measure; experience is not a randomized training intervention.

methodological_limits: The supplied article extends the 2025b report of the same experiment. The prior report, journal article and arXiv revision must not be counted as three independent participant samples.
Only 28 people contribute 560 repeated assessments. Mixed models include participant intercepts but no reported case random intercept; 560 is not the number of independent experts.

All unaided estimates precede all aided estimates by two weeks. The washout mitigates memory but does not provide counterbalanced AI order or a second unaided control, so AI effects may mix practice, session and repeat effects.
Accuracy labels for automation-bias occurrence are binary relative to a 25% threshold; percentage-error severity is a separate continuous outcome. Choosing a threshold changes which reversals count.

The approximately 7% denominator is all 560 aided assessments, not eligible initially correct/wrong-AI cases. Comparisons with published 6–11% rates require matched denominators and designs, not just numerically similar percentages.

Negative-consultation frequency and severity are explicitly descriptive because of limited filtered observations. Nineteen events per time condition do not demonstrate equivalence of rates, and severity means do not supply a significance test.

The reported repeated-measures ANOVA uses F(1,108) with 28 participants in four within-subject conditions. That degrees-of-freedom specification requires checking the analysis code before treating participant dependence as independently verified.

Overall time and AI×time performance contrasts were nonsignificant; the baseline-only decline uses a one-tailed test p=.045. A significant within-baseline result plus nonsignificant aided result does not establish a significant difference in time effects.

Positive AI weights establish association with final estimates, not inappropriate anchoring without a calibration criterion. Equal weighting is not automatically rational just because advice is well-intentioned; relative precision and dependence matter.

The normalized reliance metric uses absolute distances, so direction and overadjustment are not retained. Eleven all-identical cases were excluded for division by zero in the 549-observation model; other appendix strata total 531, not the entire 560.

Separate time-stratified regression coefficients do not by themselves test a coefficient difference. The paired normalized-reliance comparison is a different statistic and retains that metric's limitations.

Experience bins are numerically coded 0–3 and entered with one coefficient, despite being called dummy coding. This assumes a linear ordered-step relation and does not estimate independent effects for each experience category.
Baseline confidence's p=.050 and interval reaching zero are borderline; the discussion's categorical support for a protective self-efficacy effect is stronger than this estimate alone warrants.
Experience, confidence and reliance are observationally associated. More experience can also reduce beneficial advice uptake; lower reliance is not universally better.

The detector version was selected for highest average precision on the test set, according to the methods. This compromises use of that test score as an untouched generalization estimate; it does not itself establish participant bias.
Dataset annotations were reportedly verified by at least one expert, not error-free ground truth. Histology context, full-slide navigation and real treatment consequences were absent.
Prototype explanations and detection overlays accompanied predictions and were not independently varied. Influence cannot be assigned uniquely to the numeric prediction or to explanations.

The article's historical assertion that automation bias was first introduced in a 2018 source should not be repeated as established priority: earlier automation-bias publications are cited in its own references.
Code, raw data and source datasets were not rerun or independently checked; no clinical recommendation follows from this ontology review.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Alon-Barkat tests algorithm versus consultant source labels with no objective teacher-quality truth. This study instead compares repeated expert estimates with image annotations and actual detector advice. Their operationalizations answer different questions.

Shrestha uses an expert-majority benchmark and lay participants; this study uses pathology professionals and cell-count references. Neither supports generalizing a single time-pressure, accountability or advice effect to every professional context.

Kücking associates training/diagnostic ability with fewer wrong-advice agreements, but here experience relates to a general reliance proxy. These are not identical evidence for a causal training remedy.

deferred.reason: A potentially distinct construct, but here equated with one task-confidence measure. Await an original definition and discriminating measurement rather than add a broad trait from that proxy.
An operational error event within automation bias, not a separate independent psychological mechanism.
A theoretical framework cited to explain experience effects; not separately validated by this study or itself an observed behaviour.
The source names advice discounting, but does not independently establish egocentric motive. Do not automatically add the stronger label as a synonym.

limitations: One advice-integration concept added with a clear boundary between relative weighting and inappropriate discounting.
Aggregate benefit, negative threshold reversals, repeated-data provenance, metric limits and uncertain mechanism claims remain visible.
